messages.author: d3aaa07872b9962c
messages.subject: Using a background image
parts:
Hello,

Is there any chance of using a background image (e.g. from a PNG file)
for a ggplo2 plot? Maybe with a custom geom or something? This would
be needed for the purpose of plotting on a raster map. geom_tile would
be sufficient for my purposes (plotting separately read pixels) if
only it were a couple magnitudes faster and less memory-consuming.

-- Osmo

messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Re: Using a background image
parts:
Hi,

I suppose you could define a custom grob to use for the
panel.background object, though I don't know if you gain much in
efficiency,

require(pixmap)
require(RGraphics)

pixmapGrob <-
function (pic, x=0.5, y=0.5, ...)
{
pic = as(pic, "pixmapIndexed")
width = unit(pic@bbox[3], "points")
height = unit(pic@bbox[4], "points")
Z <- pic@index[nrow(pic@index):1, ,
drop = FALSE]
vp <-
viewport(x=x, y=y)
child <-
imageGrob(nrow(Z), ncol(Z), col=pic@col[Z], gp=gpar(col=NA),
by=FALSE, vp=vp, ...)

gTree(width= convertUnit(width, "in", val=TRUE),
height=convertUnit(height, "in", val=TRUE) ,
children=gList(child), childrenvp=vp, cl="pixmap")

}


background = function(){
x <- read.pnm(system.file("pictures/logo.ppm", package="pixmap")[1])
pixmapGrob(x)
}

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10)

p <- qplot(x,y,data=d) + theme_bw() +
opts(panel.background = background)

(result attached)

An alternative option could be to use the tikzDevice package, which
might let you insert a picture during the latex processing of the tikz
commands (here latex would definitely be much faster than R for a
large image). The tricky part is positioning (the tikzDevice vignette
has an example of annotations).

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Using a background image
parts:
Glad if it helps. Note that you could also use EBImage to import the
image file, using a wider range of formats (e.g. png, jpeg, gif, etc)

require(RGraphics)
require(EBImage)

ebimageGrob <-

function (pic, x=0.5, y=0.5, ...)
{

dims <- dim(pic)
colours = t(channel(pic, "x11"))
colours <- colours[ rev(seq_len(nrow(colours))), ]
width = unit(dims[1], "points")
height = unit(dims[2], "points")

vp <-
viewport(x=x, y=y)
child <-
imageGrob(dims[2], dims[1], col=colours, gp=gpar(col=colours),

by=FALSE, vp=vp, ...)

gTree(width= convertUnit(width, "in", val=TRUE),
height=convertUnit(height, "in", val=TRUE),

children=gList(child), cl="ebimage")

}

pic <- readImage("http://blog.meebo.com/imgs/map.png")
#g1 <- ebimageGrob(pic)
#dev.new(width=g1$width, height=g1$height)
#grid.draw(g1)

background = function(){
ebimageGrob(pic)
}

dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]
str(dsmall)
d <- ggplot(dsmall, aes(carat, price)) +
geom_point()+
opts(panel.background = background)


baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Using a background image
parts:
Hi all,

Regarding this old subject, Paul Murrell announced (*) a new set of
functions to deal with raster graphics in R. Using the dev version of
R, one can now do this,

require(pixmap)

as.raster.pixmapRGB <- function(x) {
nr <- nrow(x@red)
r <- rgb((x@red), (x@green), (x@blue))
dim(r) <- x@size
r
}

picture <- read.pnm(system.file("pictures/logo.ppm", package="pixmap")[1])

background = function(picture){
function() rasterGrob(picture)

}

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10)

p <- qplot(x,y,data=d) + theme_bw() +

opts(panel.background = background(picture))

I imagine it will be possible to use these new and exciting tools to:

- create filling patterns (e.g. for bw histograms)
- make general filling gradients
- combine the advantages of vector and raster graphics for large
images (the axes and text could be vector, whilst the many tiles could
be converted to raster for better rendering and huge improvement in
file size).


(*) http://developer.r-project.org/Raster/raster-RFC.html


Best,

baptiste

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Re: Using a background image
parts:
On Tue, Dec 1, 2009 at 09:54, baptiste auguie <bapt...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> - combine the advantages of vector and raster graphics for large
> images (the axes and text could be vector, whilst the many tiles could
> be converted to raster for better rendering and huge improvement in
> file size).

That would be immensely cool! geom_tile can be quite slow when
rendering many facets and at least some of it looks to me to be due to
the actual rendering of vector objects on screen. In addition, as you
mention, many PDF renderers (including Adobe's own Reader) show white
space between tiles due to antialiasing and this looks ugly.

Maybe there could be a threshold value on the number of tiles in
geom_tile, set to a sensible default but user accessible, over which
tiles are rendered as an image.

Just a thought,

JiHO
---

> rendering many facets and at least some of it looks to me to be due to

Another really problematic issue with grid.rect() is the size of the
pdf output for large images,

d <- volcano

cols <- grey(t(d)/max(c(d)))
xy <- expand.grid(x=seq(0, 1, length=ncol(d)), y=seq(0, 1, length=nrow(d)))

rect2raster <- function(g){

with(g, rasterGrob(matrix(gp$fill, ncol=length(unique(x))), mean(x),mean(y)))
}

g1 <- rectGrob(xy$y, rev(xy$x), 1/(nrow(d)), 1/(ncol(d)),
gp=gpar(col=NA, fill=cols))

g2 <- rect2raster(g1)

system.time({
pdf("comparison-rect.pdf", width=10, height=10/2*ncol(d)/nrow(d))
replicate(10, grid.draw(g1))
dev.off()
})
## user system elapsed
## 0.336 0.019 0.364
formatC(file.info("comparison-rect.pdf")$size)
## "2.36e+06"

system.time({
pdf("comparison-raster.pdf", width=10, height=10/2*ncol(d)/nrow(d))
replicate(10, grid.draw(g2))
dev.off()
})
## user system elapsed
## 0.049 0.004 0.053
formatC(file.info("comparison-raster.pdf")$size)
## "3.23e+05"

> Maybe there could be a threshold value on the number of tiles in
> geom_tile, set to a sensible default but user accessible, over which
> tiles are rendered as an image.

I think the user should be able to choose whether he wants raster or
not regardless of the number of tiles, but maybe the default could
depend on the number of tiles as you suggest.

One question is what to do when the tiles are not all of the same
size? Should this case be treated with grid.raster() also (it would
require some kind of interpolation I guess)?

Best,

baptiste
